entry.name: Shadoof
entry.desc: The shadoof is a tool for lifting water from a well, river or pond onto land or into a channel: a long pole pivoted on an upright frame, with a bucket at one end and a counterweight of clay or stone at the other. The earliest evidence of it is a cylinder seal from Mesopotamia of about 2200 BCE; it appeared in Upper Egypt sometime after 2000 BCE and reached China around the same time. One man can lift 39 to 130 litres a minute with it, and it is still used for irrigation in Africa, Asia and parts of Europe.

row.label: Shadoof
row.contested: Some historians hold that it began on the Nile, citing tomb drawings at Thebes from 1250 BCE; another theory, with little evidence, places its origin in India.

entry.name: Noria
entry.desc: A noria is a water wheel turned by a river's current whose rim carries pots, buckets or compartments that lift water into a small aqueduct, for irrigation or to supply towns. Paddle-driven water-lifting wheels had appeared in Egypt by the 4th century BCE; the Roman architect Vitruvius described the noria in the 1st century BCE, and around 300 CE the Romans tied ceramic pots to an open-framed wheel. Muslim engineers adopted and improved it: Ibn Bassal of al-Andalus fitted a flywheel, and Ismail al-Jazari a crank in 1206. The norias of Hama in Syria were 20 metres across.

row.label: Noria
row.contested: Some accounts date the noria proper from around 300 CE, when the Romans replaced its wooden compartments with ceramic pots tied to the outside of an open-framed wheel.

entry.name: Canning
entry.desc: Canning is a method of preserving food by processing it and sealing it in an airtight container, a glass jar or a steel or tin can. In 1809 the French confectioner and brewer Nicolas Appert, answering a government prize of 12,000 francs for preserved rations for the Grande Armée, developed a way of sealing food in glass jars, and was awarded the prize in 1810. In London Peter Durand patented the tin can process in 1810, and Bryan Donkin made sealed cans of tinned wrought iron, sold chiefly to the British Army and Royal Navy. Why the food kept was explained only when Louis Pasteur showed the role of microbes.

row.label: Canning
row.contested: The Dutch navy was reported to carry salmon in tin-plated iron boxes as early as 1772; the tin can patented by Durand in 1810 was allegedly the idea of the Frenchman Philippe de Girard.

entry.name: Mechanical reaper
entry.desc: A mechanical reaper is a machine that cuts, and often gathers, grain crops at harvest. Patrick Bell built one in Scotland in 1828; in the United States Obed Hussey patented a reaper in 1833 and Cyrus McCormick a horse-drawn one in 1834, completing a design begun by his father Robert, with the aid of Jo Anderson, a man enslaved by the family. Reapers spread slowly until McCormick acquired the rights to Hussey's cutter bar around 1850. The reaper-binder of 1872 also bound the sheaves, and it was replaced in turn by the swather and the combine harvester.

row.label: Mechanical reaper
row.contested: Gallic reapers, which combed off the heads of grain, were used in Roman times in what is now France. Cyrus McCormick claimed to have invented his reaper in 1831, and an 1861 ruling of the United States Patent and Trademark Office gave much of the credit to Obed Hussey.

entry.name: Tractor
entry.desc: A tractor is an engine-powered vehicle that pulls or drives farm machinery. The first tractors were steam ploughing engines, which followed the self-propelled traction engine Thomas Aveling made in 1859; in 1889 John Charter of Illinois built the first gasoline-powered tractors, and John Froelich built another in Iowa in 1892. Dan Albone's Ivel Agricultural Motor of 1901 was the first commercially successful light petrol tractor, and Henry Ford's mass-produced Fordson of 1917 held 77% of the US market by 1923. By 1935 nearly a million tractors were in use in the United States.

row.label: Tractor
row.contested: Steam came first: Thomas Aveling made a portable engine self-propelled in 1859, and steam ploughing engines, used in pairs to haul a plough by cable, were the first tractors.

entry.name: Barbed wire
entry.desc: Barbed wire is steel fencing wire with sharp points set at intervals along its strands, used for cheap fences and, as a wire obstacle, in trench warfare. In France Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans proposed a fence of thin wire with bristling points in 1860, and Louis François Janin patented a double wire with diamond-shaped barbs in 1865. In the United States Lucien B. Smith of Kent, Ohio, received the first patent in 1867, and Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patented the modern form in 1874. It made fencing the western plains cheap, and the open range was closed amid the Fence Cutting Wars of the 1880s.

row.label: Barbed wire
row.contested: Lucien B. Smith, who received the first United States patent in 1867, is regarded as the inventor; Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans had proposed a pointed wire fence in France in 1860.

entry.name: Aquaculture
entry.desc: Aquaculture is the farming of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, algae and other aquatic organisms under controlled or semi-natural conditions. Oral tradition in China places the culture of the common carp around 2000–2100 BCE, but the earliest significant evidence is The Classic of Fish Culture, a monograph by Fan Li written around 475 BCE. Romans bred fish in ponds and farmed oysters before 100 CE, medieval monasteries took up their methods, and Hawaiians built ocean fishponds. By 1866 artificial fish hatcheries operated in Canada and the United States, and world output reached 130.9 million tonnes in 2022.

row.label: Aquaculture
row.contested: The Gunditjmara of south-western Victoria, Australia, may have raised eels at Budj Bim as early as about 4,580 BCE, though Peter Sutton disputes that their eel traps were aquaculture. Evidence from Jiahu in China, from 6200 BCE, is speculative.

entry.name: Wine
entry.desc: Wine is an alcoholic drink made by fermenting grapes. The earliest known traces of it, from about 6000 BCE, were found near Tbilisi in Georgia; jars from Hajj Firuz in Iran, of about 5000 BCE, held wine sealed with pine resin, and the Areni-1 cave in Armenia holds the oldest known winery, with a press, vats and jars from about 4100 BCE. Phoenicians and Greeks spread wine around the Mediterranean, the Romans enlarged its trade, and it became part of Jewish and Christian ritual. In the 19th century phylloxera forced the replanting of almost every vine in Europe.

row.label: Wine
row.contested: Pottery jars from Jiahu in China, of the early seventh millennium BCE, may have held a fermented drink of rice and grapes, but other fruits cannot be ruled out. The Hajj Firuz jars from Iran, of about 5000 BCE, are also called the earliest firm evidence of wine production.

entry.name: Cheese
entry.desc: Cheese is a food made by curdling milk. It was probably first made by accident, when milk was stored in bladders made of ruminants' stomachs, whose rennet curdles it. The earliest direct evidence is holed clay sieves more than seven thousand years old, from Kujawy in Poland and the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, where residues suggest cheese. Sumerian cuneiform texts of the Third Dynasty of Ur record it, remains were found in an Egyptian tomb of about 2900 BCE, the first cheese factory opened in Switzerland in 1815, and Jesse Williams began assembly-line production in New York in 1851.

row.label: Cheese
row.contested: Holed pottery from pile-dwellings on Lake Neuchatel in Switzerland, roughly eight thousand years old, is thought to come from cheese strainers; where cheese-making began is not known.

entry.name: Coffee
entry.desc: Coffee is a drink brewed from the roasted seeds of the coffee plant, which grows wild in Ethiopia. There is no confirmed evidence of it being drunk before the 15th century, when Sufis in Yemen used it to stay alert during night prayers; Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri reported that Jamal-al-Din al-Dhabhani, mufti of Aden, first adopted it around 1454. It reached Mecca, Cairo and Damascus, and the first coffeehouse in Istanbul opened in 1554. Until the end of the 17th century the Yemeni port of Mocha was its only gateway; by 1788 Saint-Domingue supplied half the world's coffee, and by 1852 Brazil was the largest producer.

row.label: Coffee
row.contested: The 10th-century physician al-Razi wrote of bunchum, which later accounts say was made from a root. Legends credit the discovery to Kaldi, a 9th-century goatherd, or to the 13th-century Sufi al-Shadhili.

entry.name: Kuk Swamp
entry.desc: Kuk Swamp is an archaeological site in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, at about 1,550 metres, some 12–13 kilometres northeast of Mount Hagen. Drainage ditches dug there from about 9,000 years ago, from major disposal channels to small field ditches, turned the swamp into grassland where taro was grown, and bananas and sugar cane were cultivated from 6,900–6,400 years ago. Studied by the Australian archaeologist Jack Golson, it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008 as one of the places where people developed agriculture independently. The Kawelka people live in the area today.

entry.name: Norfolk four-course system
entry.desc: The Norfolk four-course system is a method of crop rotation in which four crops follow one another over a four-year cycle: wheat, turnips, barley, and clover or ryegrass. Unlike the earlier three-field system, it has no fallow year. It was developed in the early 16th century in Waasland, in present-day northern Belgium, and popularised in the 18th century by the British agriculturist Charles Townshend. Its fodder crop, turnips, and its grazing crop, clover, allowed livestock to be kept year-round, and it was a key development in the British Agricultural Revolution.
